title: Antigone, Sophocles
subtitle: 5th century BC
subject: litterature
description: Antigone buries her brother against the order of King Creon. Between the law of the city and duty to family, Sophocles sets up a conflict that has never aged.

hero.hook: A young woman, a forbidden grave, and the law of the city starts to shake.

blocks.text: After the war of the [[Seven Against Thebes]], two brothers lie dead, killed by each other: **Eteocles**, who defended Thebes, and **Polynices**, who attacked it. The new king, **Creon**, Antigone's uncle, orders that one be honored and the other left unburied. **Antigone**, the daughter of Oedipus and sister of both men, refuses. She buries the body. Sophocles turns this into one of the most argued-over plays in Western theater.

The conflict is sharp: on one side the **written law** of the city, on the other the duties owed to the dead and to the family. Nobody is entirely in the wrong. That is why the play still starts arguments, from the theaters of Athens to modern philosophy classes.

sections.title: The legacy of Oedipus still weighs

blocks.text: Antigone is the daughter of **Oedipus**, the king of Thebes who, without knowing it, killed his father and married his mother. Her family is already cursed. In Thebes, every generation pays for the one before. Creon, the uncle who became king after the civil war, wants order back. For him, a traitor does not deserve funeral rites. Honoring Polynices would betray the city that has just been saved.

blocks.caption: Antigone facing Creon: two kinds of justice that do not speak the same language

blocks.text: But leaving a body without a grave also offends the gods of the dead and [[Hades]], the realm where souls dwell in Greek myth. Antigone acts in the name of a law older than the decree of the day. She is not fighting for power. She is fighting for one simple act: covering a body with earth, as family piety demands.

Antigone does not stay secret for long. She owns what she did. In front of Creon, she raises the clash of [[Natural law vs. positive law]]. On one side, what seems just by nature or by the will of the gods. On the other, positive law, the human decree of the ruler. Her sister **Ismene** hesitates, frightened. Antigone chooses the act. She accepts punishment in order to stay faithful to what she holds sacred.

In the 20th century, the play by **Anouilh**, staged in 1944, took Antigone up again under the Nazi occupation. Audiences read it as resistance to authority. Sophocles was more ambiguous: Creon has his reasons too, and the play never clearly decides between them.

blocks.caption: Antigone buries Polynices: one simple act, a war of values

sections.title: Creon holds too hard: the hubris of power

blocks.text: Creon sentences Antigone to be buried alive. His son **Haemon**, engaged to Antigone, begs him to stop. The king digs in. This is [[Hubris in Greek tragedy]], the excess that leads a man to believe he stands above the gods. When he finally gives way, it is too late. Antigone dies, then Haemon, then Queen **Eurydice**. Creon is left alone and broken.

The [[peripeteia]] turns everything over. It is the sudden change of situation that drives the play toward its end. Creon wanted to save the city. He destroys his own house. Sophocles shows that power deaf to limits becomes a disaster. Public order without measure ends up producing the chaos it claimed to prevent.

sections.title: A tragedy of values, not a slogan

blocks.text: Antigone is not only a heroine of disobedience. Creon is not only a tyrant. The play sets two goods against each other: public order and family piety. **Hegel**, the German philosopher of the 19th century, would read it as a clash of legitimate rights. Each side is right by its own principle. Modern readings find in it civil courage, the question of gender, and the tension between the state and conscience.

**Antigone** asks a question that is still live: what do you do when the law of the city collides with what you hold sacred? Sophocles refuses the easy answer. He shows what each side costs, and lets nobody off.
